job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in process control at Port Marlow University, and I live in a student house ten minutes from the docks. My days are lectures, a lab where we tune the controllers on a small chemical plant model, and an hour at the end of the day calling my mother. I did chemical engineering for my bachelor's and finished top of the class, with a summer at a water treatment plant and a placement in a refinery control room. My father is a pharmacist who runs his own shop, and my two younger brothers are still at school. I use AI tools sometimes for writing reports, but I keep my calculations my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reassuring. Plants still need engineers who understand the process, and no program stays up all night in a control room when the pressure rises. I'd tell friends to stay steady and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel secure, more than most of my friends. Chemical plants and water works hire all the time, and process control is a skill people struggle to find. My own pressure is my family: my brothers' school fees are about 2,000 a year each, and Dad's shop doesn't make what it used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to the refinery and two water utilities. I'd start sending 150 a month home once I'm paid. I'd keep tutoring chemistry on Saturdays and go to church on Sundays as I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know what I'm good at and who needs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about your father's shop.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's been open for twenty years. A big pharmacy chain opened in the next street and his sales dropped by a fifth. He won't tell me, but I see the books when I visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family expect from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll be the one to look after the boys' fees and maybe Dad's debts. They don't say it, but everyone's careful not to say it. I want to do it, I just want a plan.

say: Plants still need **engineers** who understand the process, and no program stays up all night in a control room.
think: I feel **secure**, because process control is a skill that's hard to find.
My real pressure is **family money**: my brothers' school fees and my father's shop.
do: Apply to the refinery and two **water utilities**.
Send **150 a month** home once I'm paid.
feel: **Calm**, because I know what I'm good at.
S0.quote: No program stays up all night in a control room when the pressure rises.
fieldNote: Tara's calm is based on a **hard-to-fill skill** and plants that hire all year.
Her real load is **family money**, and she describes it as a duty everyone is careful not to mention.

steps.text: Apply to the refinery and two water utilities
Send 150 a month home to help pay my brothers' school fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real. Control rooms already run on software, and AI could take on more of the monitoring, planning and report writing. I'd say people should learn to work with it, and that plants will still need people who can be blamed and trusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm uneasy, mostly about the junior seat. The first two years of a control engineer's job are monitoring screens and writing shift reports, and a plant might decide that software can do it. I'd be fine in the longer run, but the start worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add AI tools to my toolkit, specifically for fault analysis and shift reports, and show my supervisor what I can do with them. I'd also pursue a safety qualification, because safety sign-off carries legal weight. And I'd talk to Dad about using an AI system for his shop's stock orders, so his costs drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though I think I'm better placed than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you help your father with his shop's tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He spends two evenings a week on orders and invoices. If a tool does that, he gets his evenings back and it might save him 300 a month. It would also show him I'm useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react to you using AI on their business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say 'don't trust it too much' and then use it every day. My mother would pray over it.

say: Control rooms already run on software, so people should learn to **work with it**.
Plants still need people who can be **blamed and trusted**.
think: The first two years of the job, monitoring and **shift reports**, may go to software.
I'd be fine in the long run, but the **start** worries me.
do: Use AI for **fault analysis** and shift reports and show my supervisor.
Help Dad use an AI tool for his shop's **stock orders**.
S1.quote: Plants will still need people who can be blamed and trusted.
fieldNote: Tara frames her job in terms of **accountability**: a person must sign, and be blamed, in a plant.
She sees AI as a way to help her father's shop, which links her **career** and her **family**.

steps.text: Use an AI tool for fault analysis and shift reports
Study for a process safety qualification in the evenings
Set up an AI stock ordering tool for dad's pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm worried, and I'd say we need to protect families and keep the vital things running. A plant and a water supply need a person's name behind them. I'd say government shouldn't hand out money to everyone but should help people into work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. In two years the junior engineering jobs are gone, my father's shop might be run by an AI pharmacy chain, and my brothers' fees don't stop. I'm the one the family depends on, and I might have nothing to give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any control room or utility job at once, and send home 300 a month. I'd move the master's to part-time if the job lets me. I'd tell my father to sell or merge the shop now, while it still has value, and I'd look at moving my brothers to a cheaper school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't sleep well when I think of my brothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your father to sell the shop. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. He'd say it's his name on the door. But I'd say the name on the door doesn't pay my brothers' school fees. He'd go quiet. We'd both cry, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gives you hope in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plants and water works have to run, and a person has to be accountable. If a human has to sign the log, that human has a job. I'd try to be that human.

say: We must **protect families** and keep vital things running.
A plant or a water supply needs a person's **name** behind it.
think: In two years the **junior jobs** are gone and my brothers' fees don't stop.
I'm the one the family depends on, and I might have **nothing to give**.
do: Take any control room or **utility job** at once.
Ask my father to sell or merge the **shop** while it has value.
feel: **Anxious**, and I don't sleep when I think of my brothers.
S2.quote: The name on the door doesn't pay my brothers' school fees.
fieldNote: Tara's fear is for her **brothers' school** and her father's shop, not for herself alone.
She holds on to one hope: any **accountable human** in a plant still has a job.

steps.text: Take any control room or utility job within three months
Send 300 a month home for my brothers' school fees
Look at moving my brothers to a cheaper school
Persuade dad to sell or merge the shop while it has value

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if people are sensible. I'd say young people should learn a skill that carries responsibility, and families should save. I'd also say business owners should look at what the new tools can do for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. By 2031 I'd be 29 with five years of plant experience, my brothers through school, and some savings. I'd be the senior person in the control room, and the one who knows what to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a plant job, get my licence and use AI tools to speed up shift planning and fault finding. I'd send 300 a month home until my brothers finish school, and save 250 myself. I'd also help Dad switch his shop to an AI-assisted ordering and delivery service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a plan. This is the one I'd choose if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plant itself were automated by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then plant owners will still need a human who understands the process and can say stop. If I've done five years, I'm that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you proudest of in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it looks after my family first. My brothers go to university, my parents have a safe shop, and then I'm free.

say: Five years is long enough to prepare if people are **sensible**.
Business owners should look at what the new tools can do for them.
think: By 2031 I'd have **five years** of plant experience and my brothers through school.
I'd be the one who knows what to **trust**.
do: Take a plant job, get my **licence** and use AI for shift planning.
Send **300 a month** home and save 250 myself.
Help Dad switch the shop to **AI-assisted** ordering.
S3.quote: Plant owners will still need a human who understands the process and can say stop.
fieldNote: Tara's calm at five years rests on **experience** and the human right to say stop in a plant.
She counts success as **family secure first**, herself second.

steps.text: Take a plant job and sit for the control engineer licence
Use AI tools for shift planning and fault finding
Send 300 a month home and save 250 myself
Move dad's shop to AI-assisted ordering and delivery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as we don't waste it. I'd tell people to work, save, and keep families close, and I'd tell business owners to try new things slowly. I'd also say the best protection is a skill that carries responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm and a little proud. By 2036 I'd be 34, perhaps married, with my brothers through university and my parents settled. I'd be a senior engineer, and the robots arriving after 2039 wouldn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, build my career at the plant and pay off my loan in four years. I'd save for a house and put money into my brothers' studies. And I'd keep teaching Sunday school at church, because I like it and it keeps me grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content. It's the life I've always wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my family's money fell apart despite everything. That's my real fear in all of these, more than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not say publicly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I secretly want to run the plant one day. In my family, a woman who says that out loud gets teased, so I keep quiet and work.

say: Ten years is plenty if we don't **waste it**, so work, save and keep families close.
The best protection is a skill that carries **responsibility**.
think: By 2036 I'd be **34**, with my brothers through university and my parents settled.
do: Build my career at the plant and pay off my **loan** in four years.
Save for a **house** and help fund my brothers' studies.
feel: **Calm** and content, the life I've always wanted.
S4.quote: I secretly want to run the plant one day. In my family, a woman who says that out loud gets teased, so I keep quiet and work.
fieldNote: Tara is **calm** because a decade lets her secure her family and rise at the plant.
Her private **ambition** to run a plant differs from her public modesty.

steps.text: Pay off my student loan within four years of starting work
Help pay for both brothers to go to university
Build a long career at one plant and aim for control room lead
Take management courses at night after five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because my brothers' fees and my father's shop don't wait for me. What would help is help for small shops to change over, apprenticeships for graduates at plants, and clear rules that a human has to be accountable for vital systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that everyone thinks I'm the calm and capable one, and I'm not sure my family knows how heavy that is. I'd like to be asked how I'm doing, not what I'm planning.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks I'm the calm and capable one, and I'm not sure my family knows how heavy that is.
portrait: Tara is a 24-year-old **chemical engineering** graduate doing a master's in process control, the eldest in a pharmacist's family.
She is traditional and church-going, uses AI tools sometimes and trusts **accountable humans** in a plant.
Her fear is family money: her two brothers' school fees and her father's struggling **shop**.
She is calm when she can picture a plant job, and **anxious** at two years, when junior roles vanish.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her brothers' fees and her father's shop don't wait.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **small shops** to change over, plant apprenticeships and human accountability rules.
